changes.before: Change super(name) to super(). What happens?
changes.after: A child class can call the parent version of a method with super.

before: class Detail < Base establishes inheritance. Detail defines its own label method, so that implementation is selected for a Detail receiver.
super(name) calls the next implementation with that argument. Bare super forwards the current arguments; super() forwards none. This distinction matters when the parent requires an argument.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
class Base
  def label(name)
    "base:#{name}"
  end
end
class Detail < Base
  def label(name)
    super(name) + "!"
  end
end
puts Detail.new.label("map")
```
Expected output or behavior: base:map!. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
Optional local transfer task: Use an explicit different string argument to super and trace the label. You may trace it without a Ruby interpreter; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

Get the parent's label before adding the child's exclamation mark.

Follow the labeled parts of this example.
```ruby
class Base
  def label(name)
    "base:#{name}"
  end
end
class Detail < Base
  def label(name)
    super(name) + "!"
  end
end
puts Detail.new.label("map")
```
The output is `base:map!`. The parent supplies base:map and the child adds the final mark.
